summary: Describes a mechanism built on TLS or DTLS that lets a peer prove ownership of an identity, such as an X.509 certificate. The proof can be exported by one peer, sent out of band, and checked by the other peer. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: You show a badge on an existing phone call and later hand over a signed note to prove it was you. The other person can check the note belongs to that same conversation.

questions: how to prove identity after a tls handshake
subtitle: Prove you own a certificate on an existing TLS connection, at any time after the handshake, without changing TLS itself.

tldr.problem: TLS authenticates peers during the handshake, but endpoints sometimes need to prove additional identities, or authenticate in response to application events, after the connection is already up.
tldr.mechanism: Either peer exports an authenticator built from Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished messages bound to the connection by exporter values, and sends it at the application layer for the other peer to validate.
tldr.outcome: Applications get post-handshake authentication, for multiple identities or on demand, without TLS-layer changes or renegotiation. It is a building block, so applications handle advertising support and errors themselves.

today: RFC 9261 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Authenticating After the Handshake
sections.content:
RFC 9261 lets one party of a TLS or DTLS connection authenticate to its peer using messages created after the session is established. Client and server can prove ownership of additional identities at any time after the handshake. The proof is exported by one party, sent out of band, and validated by the peer.

The RFC names two advantages over native TLS authentication: multiple identities (an endpoint with no single certificate covering all its identities can authenticate additional ones over one connection) and spontaneous authentication (endpoints can authenticate in response to higher-layer events, with more application context).

It can replace the post-handshake client authentication that older TLS versions did with renegotiation, and, unlike renegotiation, it needs no changes at the TLS layer. TLS 1.3 has its own post-handshake authentication, but that needs extra TLS state and aligns with TLS record boundaries, which do not match the boundaries of protocols such as HTTP/2. The minimum versions are TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2. Exported Authenticators are a building block: advertising support and handling authentication errors are left to the application.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS normally checks who you are only when the call starts. This lets you prove more about yourself later, without hanging up and redialing.

sections.title: Message Sequences and Requests
sections.content:
Two message types exist: authenticator requests and authenticators. They combine into three sequences.

  • Client Authentication: the server generates a request, the client generates an authenticator from it, the server validates it.
  • Server Authentication: the client generates a request, the server answers with an authenticator, the client validates it.
  • Spontaneous Server Authentication: the server generates an authenticator with no request, and the client validates it.

A server-generated request uses the TLS 1.3 CertificateRequest structure. A client-generated request uses a new message, ClientCertificateRequest, with the same structure (it is a certificate request made by the client, not a request for a client certificate). Both are used even on TLS 1.2 or DTLS 1.2, are encoded as handshake messages without record-layer framing, and are not encrypted with a handshake or application-data key.

The certificate_request_context (0 to 255 octets) identifies the request and is echoed in the authenticator. It MUST be unique for each request within a connection, and SHOULD be unpredictable, for example random, so an attacker with temporary access to a private key cannot precompute authenticators. The extensions are those marked CR in the TLS ExtensionType registry, and a client request MAY also include server_name. Requests SHOULD travel over a channel with security equivalent to TLS, such as QUIC; the existing connection MAY be used.
sections.plainLanguage: One side can ask 'prove it', or the server can volunteer proof on its own. Each question carries a unique label so an old answer cannot be replayed.

sections.title: Building an Authenticator
sections.content:
An authenticator is built from an established connection, an identity such as an X.509 certificate, and its private key. It is the concatenation Certificate || CertificateVerify || Finished, each encoded as a TLS handshake message. Clients MUST NOT send an authenticator without a preceding request; for servers a request is optional.

  • Certificate carries the end-entity certificate and any chain, plus the certificate_request_context from the request (or an unpredictable, unique value if none). It MUST only contain extensions present in the request, or in the ClientHello if there was no request. Only X.509 is supported; Raw Public Keys are not.
  • CertificateVerify is explicit proof of private key possession. The signature scheme MUST be valid for TLS 1.3, which excludes all RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 algorithms. The signature covers 64 copies of octet 32, the context string "Exported Authenticator", a single 0 octet, and the hash of Handshake Context, request and Certificate.
  • Finished is an HMAC over the hash of Handshake Context, request, Certificate and CertificateVerify, keyed with the Finished MAC Key.

An authenticator is valid if CertificateVerify is correctly constructed and Finished matches the expected value. Validators SHOULD use constant-time comparisons for the signature and MAC. If the endpoint has no suitable identity or does not want to answer, it sends an empty authenticator: a Finished message alone, as an authenticated refusal.
sections.plainLanguage: The note has three parts: your ID card, a signature showing you really own it, and a stamp proving it was made for this exact conversation. Saying 'no thanks' is also stamped.

sections.title: Tying It to the Connection
sections.content:
Each authenticator uses a Handshake Context and a Finished MAC Key derived from the connection with a TLS exporter (RFC 5705 for TLS 1.2, RFC 8446 for TLS 1.3, where exporter_master_secret MUST be used, not early_exporter_master_secret). The labels depend on who sends: EXPORTER-client authenticator handshake context, EXPORTER-server authenticator handshake context, EXPORTER-client authenticator finished key and EXPORTER-server authenticator finished key. The exporter context value is empty for all four, and the output length equals the hash output length of the ciphersuite.

Because these values come from the connection, an authenticator generated on a different connection will not validate. The RFC notes this includes cases where application data passes through a TLS-terminating proxy. Exported Authenticators cannot be used with ciphersuites lacking the needed hash, and to avoid key synchronization attacks they MUST NOT be generated or accepted on (D)TLS 1.2 connections that did not negotiate the extended master secret extension (RFC 7627).
sections.plainLanguage: The stamp is made from secrets only the two people on this call share. A note made on a different call will not carry the right stamp.

sections.title: API Considerations
sections.content:
Creating and validating requests and authenticators SHOULD be implemented inside the (D)TLS library, even though it could be done in the application. Implementations SHOULD offer APIs, described informatively as four calls.

  • request: takes a context (0 to 255 octets) and a set of extensions that MUST include signature_algorithms, and returns a request.
  • get context: returns the certificate_request_context of a request or authenticator.
  • authenticate: takes the connection, an identity, a signer and a request or context, and returns an authenticator or an empty authenticator.
  • validate: takes the connection, an optional request, an authenticator and a certificate chain validation function, and returns whether it is valid plus the identity if so.

All APIs MUST fail on (D)TLS 1.1 or earlier, or on (D)TLS 1.2 without the extended master secret. Validation should fail if the context was already used by a previously validated authenticator, and well-formed empty authenticators are returned as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: A good TLS toolkit should give programmers four buttons: ask for proof, read the label, make proof, and check proof.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished pattern deliberately mirrors the TLS 1.3 pattern, which has been analyzed several times. Authenticators are independent and unidirectional, and nothing changes inside TLS when one is created or validated. That makes it hard to formally prove a server is jointly authoritative over multiple identities, and TLS gives no indication of when an authenticator was computed, so any timing must be tracked by the application.

The signature covers the context string "Exported Authenticator", so it cannot be transplanted into other protocols. In TLS 1.3 a client cannot learn whether its Finished was accepted, so servers MUST verify the client Finished message before sending or processing an Exported Authenticator.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only works for this kind of conversation, and the server must make sure the call is truly set up before trusting any note.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content: IANA updated three TLS registries. In the ExtensionType registry, server_name(0) now lists "CH, EE, CR", where CR only marks it as valid in a ClientCertificateRequest. Four exporter labels were added to the TLS Exporter Labels registry, with DTLS-OK and Recommended set to Y. In the HandshakeType registry, client_certificate_request (17) was added with DTLS-OK set to Y and the comment "Used in TLS versions prior to 1.3".
sections.plainLanguage: The official lists of TLS names and numbers got a few new entries so everyone uses the same labels.

data.title: Authenticator and Finished
data.code:
Authenticator = Certificate || CertificateVerify || Finished

Finished = HMAC(Finished MAC Key, Hash(Handshake Context ||
     authenticator request || Certificate || CertificateVerify))
